name: Dogon masks and the Dama ceremony
subtitle: Among the Dogon, masks are carved by initiates of the Awa mask society and danced at funerary rites; the dama is the large ceremony that ends mourning.

facts.label: What
facts.value: Mask dances are the highlight of post-burial rites, including the elaborate dama ceremonies held for men that mark the end of mourning.

facts.label: Who makes
facts.value: The masks are carved away from the village by the initiates of the Awa, the society of masks.

facts.label: When
facts.value: The Awa societies of different villages meet for the Dama between three and five years after the funeral (as described by Quai Branly).

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: The Dama is reserved for deceased men and exceptionally women, and brings together between 100 and 400 masks.

facts.label: Who dances
facts.value: In principle all children and almost all women are prohibited from approaching masks; a select group of female initiates are the exception.

facts.label: Other uses
facts.value: Mask dances are also part of official celebrations such as school and clinic openings, and in peak holiday season are performed for tourists for a fee.

facts.label: Risk
facts.value: UNESCO, quoted by AFP, said the gradual disappearance of cultural practices such as traditional funerary rituals and masked dances fuelled intercommunal strife in Bandiagara.

facts.label: Heritage status
facts.value: The Cliff of Bandiagara (Dogon land) was placed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1989.

parts.text: Among the Dogon, masks are carved by initiates of the Awa mask society and danced at funerary rites; the dama is the large ceremony that ends mourning. Masks also appear at official celebrations and, for a fee, for tourists. UNESCO links the loss of funerary rituals and masked dances to the conflict in the region.
